title: Cycling Time Calculator: Ride Duration Estimator
description: Estimate how long a ride takes from distance and expected speed with the Cycling Time Calculator — honest about stops and terrain. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, 68 km at a steady 21 km/h takes about 3 hours 14 minutes of riding — the figure a café stop then extends, by exactly the length of the stop.
quick_answer: The Cycling Time Calculator divides a route's distance by the average speed you expect to hold and returns the ride's duration. Enter the distance from your route plan and a realistic average, and read the time — then add your stops deliberately instead of discovering them at dusk.
steps_intro: Time is distance wearing the speed you can actually hold. Be honest in both inputs:

body.t: A winter ride must fit the light. Distance from the
history, answer here — before the ride, not during it.
Publish a finish time built from the group's true average, not the leader's. The group's average is the slowest honest number in the chain.
Can you ride to the 9 a.m. meeting? The estimate with your real average — plus changing time — is the professional answer.
Touring days are sized in hours, then converted to kilometres by this division. Five riding hours at 20 km/h is a 100 km day, whatever the map wishes.
68 km at 21 km/h = 3.24 h ≈ 3 h 14 min of riding. Add two 15-minute stops and the door-to-door is 3 h 44 min — the second figure is the one to tell the family.
100 miles at 16 mph = 6 h 15 min riding. Centuries are won by the average held at mile 80, not the one boasted at mile 8 — the calculator takes the average you give it.

faq: Does this replace a specialist tool or professional measurement?
No — it divides distance by your stated average. Route computers estimate from terrain and your history; this is the transparent version you can argue with.
Is my input uploaded?
No. The estimate is computed in your browser.
Does the route include live traffic?
No. Junctions and towns are inside your average if your average came from real rides — another reason to use your own history, not a hope.
Why is road distance longer than straight-line?
Roads wind, and you ride roads. Plan with the routed distance from the Cycling Route Planner.
Can route results change over time?
Your average changes with fitness and season. Recompute with the current rider, not last summer's.
Should stops be included?
Deliberately, as additions. The calculator gives riding time; the day is riding time plus stops, and only you know your café discipline.
What average should a beginner use?
A completed ride's average — from the Cycling Speed Calculator over a known distance — beats any chart. Until then, 15 km/h is a kinder planning assumption than 25.
Headwind forecast — what changes?
Your sustainable average, by a lot. Drop the input speed honestly (riders often lose 3–5 km/h to a strong headwind) and the plan survives the weather.
Can I plan a relay or audax leg with it?
Yes — each leg is a distance and an average. Chain the legs and add the controls' stoppage time as additions.
Why is my real time always longer?
Stops, junctions and the average decaying late in the ride. Add 10–15% to the rolling figure for a door-to-door truth, calibrated by your own history.
